newsitem.title: UK: William Hill hangs up "for sale" sign.
newsitem.headline: William Hill hangs up "for sale" sign.

text.p: Close Brothers, merchant bank to debt-laden Brent Walker Group Plc, is inviting offers for William Hill, the group's last significant asset and Britain's second largest betting shop chain, William Hill said on Tuesday.

"A memo of information has gone out to interested parties seeking indicative offers and at that stage the board of Brent Walker will decide if they are going to proceed and if they proceed whether that will be for a sale or a float," William Hill managing director John Brown said in an interview.

Potential buyers have until the beginning of July to put in their indicative offers. Analysts put a price of between 500 and 600 million pounds ($832-$999 million) on the business. It is valued on Brent Walker's books at 428 million.
Brewer-to-leisure-group Bass Plc declined to comment on mounting press speculation that the group is poised to make an offer.
"We don't comment on market speculation," said a Bass spokesman.
But analysts said William Hill would fit well with Bass's own chain of 890 Coral betting shops and produce sizeable cost savings.
"The only problem is the obvious monopoly concerns," said one analyst.
If the government allowed the deal to go ahead it would give Bass 35 percent of a market valued at about 6.0 billion pounds a year. Ladbroke Group Plc has 1,915 shops and William Hill 1,550.

"It is no coincidence that Bass was very cautious in its remarks after Beckett (Margaret Beckett, Trade and Industry Secretary) turned down its bid for Carlsberg-Tetley. Obviously they know they will have to go back to her in the near future," he added.
William Hill is Brent Walker's last major asset after the sale of the Pubmaster chain of inns in November for 171 million pounds.

Brent Walker's loan covenants with its banks, owed some 1.3 billion pounds by the company, draw to a close at the end of the year. Brent Walker, built up by former boxer George Walker, was rescued from collapse by its banks in 1991 at the height of recession.

But William Hill, ring-fenced from its parent, has shown a marked improvement recently to report a 30 percent increase in trading profit to 50.3 million in 1996. Analysts expect a strong set of first-half figures due in September.
The whole gaming and betting industry is now an altogether more attractive business and expanding quickly against the background of government relaxation of gaming laws.

A reduction in the government betting levy and the introduction of fruit machines to betting shops have helped bookmakers to recover after they were badly hit by the launch of the national lottery in 1994.
Hotel and leisure group Ladbroke said in May that pretax profits for the first four months of 1997 were well ahead of the year-ago period.
In an update on trading the group said its betting and gaming division was performing strongly, benefiting from the introduction of new products like amusement-with-prizes machines in its shops.
Coral reported a near doubling of profits to 15 million stg in the half-year to April 12. Where Bass has refurbished Coral's and renamed them Blue Shops, turnover has improved.
William Hill, which has about half its shops in the London area, is currently about seven years through a 10 year refurbishment programme across its estate.
Bass shares were up seven pence at 742 by 1200 GMT and Ladbroke three pence higher at 237.
($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
